This momentum space is constructed from the position space through dual derived smooth structures, resulting in a natural way to represent momentum maps and their corresponding generalized forms. This in turn facilitates a natural transformation between generalized Poincaré forms and their duals in momentum space, providing a method to integrate conservation laws into Einstein's vacuum equations without directly applying them. This approach has been further refined to incorporate a generalized version of Weyl's double d operator, providing a method to obtain a self-dual and anti-self-dual decomposition of generalized Poincaré forms and their corresponding duals in momentum space. This decomposition effectively provides a natural way to represent the self-dual and anti-self-dual parts of the Einstein vacuum equations without directly applying them.

In the finite field of order $q^3$, a new category of permutation polynomials is being examined, specifically the $\sigma$-permutation polynomials, where $\sigma$ is the Frobenius automorphism defined by $\sigma(x)=x^q$. Certain subgroups of the group of permutation polynomials are identified, each consisting of new families of permutation polynomials. These include subgroups composed of generalized Dickson polynomials and their compositions with monomials, as well as permutations derived from various polynomial forms. The application of Walsh-Spencer representation and cross-correlation values of the associated functions associated with these permutation polynomials are also discussed.

Enteric parasites pose a significant global health risk, with infections linked to
malnutrition, seizures, and intestinal blockages. Although current diagnostic
techniques are relatively simple, they often require multiple stool samples to
detect an infection, as a single test may yield false negatives. In this study, we
utilize the publicly available MIMIC EEG dataset to develop a novel enteric
parasite prediction model, EntericNet, which utilizes raw multi-channel EEG
signals. The model's architecture consists of three sequential stages: a channel
selector that identifies the most informative EEG channels, a feature extractor
that captures relevant patterns, and a classifier that predicts parasite
infections. By employing these techniques, we demonstrate the potential of
enteric parasite classification using enteroencephalogram EEG signals.

This study explores a Procrustean game of stochastic differential investment and reinsurance, which also takes into account Pro-rata and loss-limiting reinsurance policies. By applying a verification theorem, it's been demonstrated that the value functions' solutions to the associated Crandall-Itona solution of a Procrustean game, which also satisfies a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system, constitute equilibrium strategies. A characterization of the value functions is provided, along with an analysis of the effect of various model parameters on the reinsurance threshold.

This study presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control strategy integrated with a Kalman Filter to enhance quadcopter flight stability and precision. The quadcopter model is linearized and employed to design the PIDA controller in the time domain. The Kalman Filter is then integrated to mitigate noise and optimize tracking performance. The proposed control strategy is tested on two quadcopter models: the T-Bug and the Fixed-Wing, with the T-Bug model utilized for simulating and validating results. The research demonstrates that the PIDA-Kalman Filter combination yields superior performance compared to conventional controllers.

A thorough examination of the scientific literature reveals that the chiral effective field theory provides a precise and systematic framework for understanding pion-nucleon interactions at low energy. Building on this concept, a new deep learning model, the Chiral Effective Field Theory Convolutional Neural Network (CEFT-CNN), has been developed. This model integrates the chiral effective field theory into a convolutional neural network, thereby capturing the symmetries and low-energy properties of QCD. We have tested the CEFT-CNN on 10 tasks related to pion-nucleon scattering, achieving superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Our research also shows that the CEFT-CNN can learn key aspects of the chiral effective field theory, such as the order-by-order expansion, power counting, and symmetry constraints. Furthermore, our study provides an in-depth analysis of the CEFT-CNN's performance under various conditions.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) tracking system at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC) incorporates the silicon pixel detector as its core component, enabling precise tracking of particle interactions. This study outlines a method for refining the position of the CMS pixel detector using data from particle collisions. By analyzing the curvature of charged particles in the detector's presence of a magnetic field, a specialized algorithm has been developed to enhance the accuracy of the pixel detector. This method provides a per-track correction, effectively removing environmental distortions caused by the detector's own electronics. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations and real-world data, resulting in a significant improvement in track positioning.

Our research examines the physical properties of 12,000 Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN)  hosts, spanning redshifts 0.02 to 2.5, using a combination of observational data and spectral energy distribution fitting. We leverage the zCOSMOS galaxy survey's redshift measurements and the SDSS r-band magnitudes to assess the AGN host physical properties. Our analysis focuses on the relationship between the star formation rate and redshift of the AGN host, as well as the correlation between the stellar mass and redshift. We also explore the morphological classification of the AGN hosts, employing the Hubble type system. Our results reveal that the star formation rate of the AGN hosts peaks at a redshift of approximately 1.2 and then declines, while the stellar mass of the AGN hosts reaches a maximum at a redshift of approximately 1.5. Our research indicates that the morphological type of the AGN hosts is predominantly spiral, with a significant fraction of elliptical galaxies. Our findings are compared with those of previous studies, and our research contributes to the understanding of the co-evolution of the AGN and its host galaxy.

High-energy and high-momentum fluctuations within a nucleus arise from short-range correlations between nucleons. These correlations can be observed in high-momentum behavior of nucleons, as well as in high-momentum transfers in exclusive reactions. This work examines the effects of short-range correlations on nuclear structure functions and the modifications of a nucleon when bound within a nucleus. We demonstrate that such correlations significantly impact the nuclear structure functions and the nuclear modification factor. Additionally, we find that they contribute to a substantial portion of a nucleus's total kinetic energy.

Complex-valued neural networks, introduced in the 80s, have primarily been overlooked in the field of machine learning. Recent studies have attempted to integrate complex components into neural networks, but they have typically treated complex numbers as real-valued, which hinders the natural flow of complex information. This paper proposes a novel complex scaling technique, allowing for the efficient representation of complex-valued functions through real-valued scaling. Based on this approach, we develop a novel complex-valued network structure, which retains complex characteristics while being easily optimized through gradient descent. Experimental results demonstrate that our complex network outperforms existing designs, achieving a 1% higher accuracy in the MNIST dataset and significantly reducing model size and computational requirements while maintaining high accuracy on the UCI dataset.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations have been instrumental in explaining various physical phenomena that occur within the saturation momentum range. As these processes vary in energy, the concept of saturation momentum becomes vital. In most cases, it is assumed that the surrounding vacuum remains static, but a more accurate understanding necessitates considering its dynamic nature. This work delves into the non-perturbative effects arising from vacuum fluctuations on the saturation momentum in both its real and imaginary components.

A thorough examination of the abundance patterns in 1,000 very metal-poor stars from Gaia-ESO Survey 1 has been conducted. The study focused on the abundance of 17 key elements, including sodium, calcium, titanium, and others, in stars with mass fractions below -2.0. The abundance data was corrected for errors and compared across different sub-samples, including FGK-type stars, and the results showed a high level of consistency. The abundance patterns were analyzed across a wide range of metallicity, and the study found that many elements exhibit significant intrinsic variability, with some reaching up to 0.4 dex. The abundance patterns were also examined across different Galactic heights and color-magnitude diagrams, and the study found that many elements exhibit anti-correlated behavior, including the well-known [α/Fe] phenomenon. The abundance patterns were compared across different sub-samples and the study found that the mean abundance patterns are consistent with previous studies, including 3-D Magellan-FORGE. The abundance patterns were analyzed in relation to the properties of the galaxies, including the mass of the bulge and the metallicity of the bulge, and the study found that the abundance patterns are consistent with the 3-D Magellan-FORGE data.

In the realm of machine learning, omitting crucial but unseen variables can result in inaccurate forecasts, ultimately harming model performance. The primary objective of our research is to develop a method for identifying and recovering unseen variables that significantly influence the target variable. Our proposed approach utilizes variational autoencoders to identify the most influential unseen variables and subsequently predicts them. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the efficacy of the recovered unseen variables in improving prediction accuracy.

We introduce and evaluate a novel hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithm, which leverages quantum computations in the form of kernel evaluations to outperform traditional methods in certain problems. To test the efficacy of this approach, we have developed and implemented two distinct quantum kernel functions, one derived from the quantum classifier proposed by Biamonte et al., and another inspired by the quantum classifier proposed by Cereceda. Our results, obtained through numerical simulations on both shortered and fully quantum devices, demonstrate the potential of the algorithm to achieve optimal performance on certain problems, including the classification of randomly generated data and the identification of MNIST digits. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the algorithm can achieve optimal performance on the latter without the need for hyperparameter tuning. Our study also reveals that the performance of the algorithm is highly dependent on the choice of parameters, including the number of qubits and the strength of the interaction Hamiltonian. Our findings provide a valuable reference for the development of quantum algorithms for machine learning.

Researchers have recently examined pointwise slant submanifolds within almost Hermitian manifolds. In this work, the authors establish necessary and sufficient conditions for such submanifolds within the Sasakian framework and derive metric connections, inducing metrics, and Gauss equations for them. Additionally, examples are provided to illustrate these concepts.

The identification of low-energy nuclear recoil events is crucial for a range of applications, including dark matter detection, astrophysics and geoneutrino research, radiometric dating, and isotope identification. A novel detection method based on the ionization produced by nuclear recoils in supercooled silicon crystals is being developed, which could potentially operate at an extremely low temperature of 0.1 Kelvin. This technique could lead to the creation of a large-scale detector made of highly pure silicon that would be sensitive enough to detect a single neutron recoil. In this study, the current status of this R&D method is presented along with the initial results obtained for the detection of individual nuclear recoil events.

We examine a model of active colloids in an environment where the interactions between the colloids and the surrounding medium are random and change with the environment's activity. A pair of active colloids moves in response to gradients of activity, exhibiting two types of behavior: it moves towards higher levels of activity and displays self-propulsion. A type of moving pattern called crawling is observed, where the colloid pair moves in response to a change in activity, as well as self-propelling motion. We investigate the characteristics of these moving patterns and the conditions under which they occur.

We've performed high-precision numerical simulations of the half-filled quantum Hall system in the presence of a 24-peak Landau level, finding that magnetoroton modes of the $1/3$ and $2/9$ states exhibit unique properties. While the $2/9$ state displays two magnetoroton peaks with distinct minima, separated by the quasiparticle-hole excitation, the $1/3$ and $2/9$ states show similar behavior. Interestingly, the $2/7$ state displays two magnetoroton peaks with overlapping minima, similar to the $1/3$ or near half filling. Our results suggest that the $2/7$ and $2/9$ quasiparticles have different internal structures, rooted in their wave functions.

Epidemics on massive networks pose significant challenges for analysis and modeling, primarily due to their scale. The onset of an outbreak is often marked by exponential growth, rendering the epidemic trajectory unpredictable and fragile. The RHAPSODES algorithm addresses these issues by dividing infected individuals into multiple clusters, each with a unique infection timeline. By doing so, RHAPSODES can utilize local analytical methods to forecast each cluster's trajectory, combining these predictions to provide a more accurate overall forecast. RHAPSODES also incorporates an adaptive approach to adjust prediction accuracy as new data becomes available, allowing it to refine its forecasts over time. The effectiveness of RHAPSODES has been demonstrated through simulations on networks of up to 10 million nodes, showcasing its ability to forecast and scale R0 values with high precision. RHAPSODES is a valuable tool for forecasting and scaling epidemic outbreaks, offering a practical solution for analyzing large-scale epidemics.

The accuracy of reconstructed maps in CMB map-making is heavily influenced by the quality of models used to describe instrument behavior. These models, however, are often imperfect, leading to errors in pixel correlations that can significantly impact the maximum likelihood estimator. To mitigate this issue, we have developed an innovative approach to quantifying and measuring these errors, leveraging stochastic sampling to accurately reflect the effects of model inaccuracies on the estimator. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of applying this method to large-scale data sets, such as Planck data, and highlight the importance of understanding and accounting for model errors in order to produce reliable map estimates.

In the context of teaching, referential ambiguity can pose challenges to effective instruction, particularly when learners misinterpret task requirements due to unclear phrasing. While teaching methods often rely on teacher-initiated clarification, student-driven solutions are also necessary. This research aims to explore how a learning agent can independently recognize and address referential ambiguities in educational settings. A proposed approach involves the use of visual object tracking and association rules to establish connections between task-related references and target objects. By integrating these elements into the design of interactive tasks, it is possible to create a framework for task automation and assessment. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through a case study involving an educational robot named NAO, where the learner's ability to perform predicted actions is a key indicator of successful referential ambiguity resolution.

Quantum process tomography is a vital technique used to characterize and verify quantum processes, which are fundamental to quantum computing and sensing. As a consequence of the increasing complexity of quantum systems, traditional quantum process tomography methods become computationally infeasible. In response, we have developed an innovative approach called quantum process estimation, which utilizes variational methods to efficiently learn the dynamics of quantum processes. This new technique, called QPE, is capable of handling high-dimensional unitary processes by utilizing a single, trainable quantum circuit. In our experiments, we have shown that our approach outperforms existing techniques in multiple scenarios, including noisy quantum circuits, quantum channel concatenation, and random quantum processes. Furthermore, we have successfully applied our method to analyze complex quantum processes, such as those found in superconducting qubit systems. Our findings suggest that quantum process estimation could become a standard tool for characterizing quantum devices in the future.

We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities for this constant in two-dimensional convex bodies and generalizing these results to convex polyhedra in three-dimensional space.

The advent of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) has generated significant interest in the field of wireless communications due to their potential to enhance coverage in areas lacking sufficient infrastructure. This paper introduces a new approach to tackle the UAV altitude optimization issue, where a novel non-linear constraint is proposed to model the optimal flying height in the context of maximizing signal coverage. By transforming this constraint into a convex problem, it is possible to derive a closed-form solution for optimal altitude, which is then incorporated into an iterative algorithm to convert the initial optimization problem into a solvable semidefinite problem. This is achieved through a combination of a change of variables and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker condition, ultimately leading to a more efficient and reliable algorithm for initial value selection and convergence. This algorithm is shown to outperform existing solutions in simulation results, demonstrating its effectiveness in optimizing UAV altitudes for maximum signal coverage.

The low-energy electronic structure of an unbiased bilayer graphene is characterized by a quadratic dispersion relation. Our study reveals that when low-energy interactions are incorporated, the dispersion relation flattens out and develops a gap, with the interaction strength directly influencing the bandgap. Our findings are based on the self-consistent solution of the Schrödinger equation for the parabolic band and a short-range Coulomb-like potential, which we verified through the convergence of our results across various interlayer distances and interaction strengths. Our research validates the self-consistent approach and demonstrates the potential for tuning interactions to manipulate the electronic properties of quadratic semiconductors, such as bilayer graphene, through external stimuli.

The electronic structure and work function of Sc2TbN@C80 and its temperature-dependent behavior were studied using temperature-dependent photoelectron spectroscopy.  Spectra taken at various temperatures revealed the unique Sc2TbN@C80 molecular orbitals and their temperature-induced shifts.  Notably, the molecule's highest occupied molecular orbital exhibited a temperature-dependent shift resulting in a work function decrease of 0.04 eV per 100 K increase.  These findings were corroborated by density functional theory calculations.

The Internet of Things (IoT) comprises a vast network of interconnected devices powered by various energy sources, with many being battery-operated and, in some cases, device replacement being impractical. Consequently, IoT devices require robust security without compromising on power efficiency. Traditional encryption methods are often unsuitable for low-powered IoT devices due to their resource-intensive nature. Therefore, there is a pressing need for innovative, power-efficient security solutions tailored for IoT applications. This paper presents an overview of the latest developments in IoT security and power efficiency, focusing on novel approaches to secure communications and the potential for integrating error correction and security functionalities to streamline processing and minimize power consumption.

The Ramsey measurement efficiency can be maximized by optimizing the phase measurement range in Ramsey experiments, a technique widely used for NISQ quantum computing, quantum sensing, and atomic physics. By extending the measurement range of a Ramsey-based spin qubit, a BLOCH-R measurement, we have demonstrated an 80% efficiency improvement, accompanied by a minimal loss of sensitivity of less than 1%. We have also successfully applied this enhanced measurement technique to detect radio frequencies with sensitivity of 2000 photons per second, achievable within 10 milliseconds.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance in various contexts. A fundamental limitation of existing centrality metrics is their inaccuracy in networks that are highly complex and contain an abundance of multi-cycle connections. This research introduces novel findings that establish a connection between Gromov centrality and a specific geometric property known as triangle inequality excess, which characterizes complex cycle networks. A comprehensive investigation is conducted to explore the relationship between this property and Gromov centrality in networks with homogeneous edge weights. Our analysis reveals that in certain network models, the average value of triangle inequality excess decreases exponentially as the network grows larger, leading to an asymptotic equivalence between Gromov centrality and a more established betweenness centrality measure. A specific network model known as random hypergraphs is also examined, demonstrating that its associated network graph exhibits small cycles and converges towards an infinite network that contains no cycles at all.

The behavior of planets in our solar system is attributed to the unique gravitational field generated by the spinning nature of the sun, which varies based on the direction of their orbital motion, while the laws of physics remain consistent under rotational symmetry, with the spacetime metric exhibiting the characteristics of a Karlovitz field, containing a singularity at the origin, exhibiting properties of both electrovac and gravitationally charged fields, with the latter displaying properties of a magnetic monopole, with the resulting gravitational force behaving as a repulsive force, with the effect of the gravitational field generated by the spinning nature of the sun being able to resolve discrepancies in planetary data, with the effect of the gravitational field generated by the spinning nature of the sun being able to explain discrepancies in planetary data, with the effect of the gravitational field generated by the spinning nature of the sun being able to resolve discrepancies in planetary data, with the effect of the gravitational field generated by the spinning nature of the sun being able to explain discrepancies in planetary data, with the effect of the gravitational field generated by the spinning nature of the sun being able to resolve discrepancies in planetary data, with the effect of the gravitational field generated by the spinning nature of the sun being able to explain discrepancies in planetary data, with the effect of the gravitational field generated by the spinning nature of the sun being able to resolve discrepancies in planetary data, with the effect of the gravitational field generated by the spinning nature of the sun being able to explain discrepancies in planetary data, with the effect

Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are categorized into equivalence classes which form the elements of a structure known as the NC-form. This complex geometric object, known as a space, can be studied through the lens of algebraic geometry. By examining the properties of a related space, we can derive insights into the topology of the NC-form, specifically its connected components. This understanding is further illustrated through the case studies of specific matrix pencil configurations.

We will demonstrate that the class of almost abelian solvmanifolds includes a diverse range of examples that support topological T-duality but lack any symplectic or cohomological duals. Additionally, we will show that no general symplectic dual symplectic bundle pair exists for the class of abelian solvmanifolds as previously proposed.

We present a new method to embed graphs of fixed diameter into the minor-free graphs H, resulting in a treewidth within H of O(n^(1/d -  ε)) for some positive constant ε, where d is the diameter. This surpasses the earlier known technique which yielded an H with treewidth of Ω(n^(1/(d + 1))) for all diameters d. This improvement is a crucial first step in resolving a long-standing query: can the treewidth bound for minor-free graphs H with diameter d be improved to O(n^(1/d))?

For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior is characterized, and discrete half-loop objects that facilitate linearization near repelling fixed points are defined, leading to a proven universality theorem that offers a structural understanding of the system's asymptotic behavior through the use of conformal hulls to facilitate conjugation within the orbits of a half-loop object.

We have developed a novel approach to construct unitary operators for closed systems by mapping a method originally used for open systems (H. Y. Zhou et al., 2021). The proposed method employs qubit-based evolutions, in contrast to the conventional fermionic-based evolutions. By doing so, it overcomes the need to handle the complexity of fermionic algebra and allows for the use of shorter time intervals in quantum simulations. We have applied this method to simulate the dynamics of two fermion particles in a double-well potential and found that it yields identical results to fermionic-based evolutions. Furthermore, our approach exhibits greater robustness when implemented on near-term quantum devices, specifically in the case of noisy superconducting quantum processors.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of deep
generative models that utilize neural networks to approximate complex
probability distributions. These models have the potential to improve the
efficiency of learning from large datasets, but they often suffer from
challenges such as poor convergence and low sample quality. To address these
issues, researchers have proposed the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD), which
utilizes a deep neural network to model a data distribution. Unlike
variational autoencoders, DGDs do not require an encoder and instead use
stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) for optimization and sampling.
By leveraging a prior distribution with unit variance, DGDs can be optimized
more efficiently and achieve better sample quality, as demonstrated in
experiments on synthetic and MNIST datasets.

The presence of a primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background in our universe's current era could be attributed to various factors, such as the early universe's rapid expansion. In our study, we examine how this background affects the universe's expansion history by comparing it against the findings of the Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo detectors, specifically looking at the GW170817 event. Our analysis reveals that if the universe's expansion is influenced by this background, it could lead to a limited duration of time before a black hole's quasinormal ringdown phase, as well as a current density of the background within a certain range.

We have analyzed the inner coma of comet C/2015 ER61 using the APEX telescope at 1.3 mm and 0.87 mm wavelengths. Our observations, conducted at a distance of 0'.25 from the cometary nucleus, have identified the cometary emissions at both wavelengths. The data also allowed us to detect the previously unidentified C2P2 molecule, in addition to the more common CO, CN, CS, CS2, and SO molecules. The measured column densities for these molecules ranged from 1.3 x 10^17 cm^-2 for CO to 3.3 x 10^16 cm^-2 for CN. The detection of C2P2, the first reported instance of this molecule in a comet, has been accompanied by the measurement of its production rate, which is estimated to be 1.3 x 10^28 s^-1. Our findings suggest that the observed coma is dominated by the nucleus outgassing, with the exception of CN, whose emission may be partially attributed to the photodissociation of NCN.

We introduce an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent advances in automatic speech recognition and speech translation, utilizing only raw, unlabeled data from speakers without requiring explicit phonetic inventories or alignment processes. Our method is entirely data-driven, requiring just audio and corresponding transcript inputs, and involves no human annotation. We evaluate the performance of the method on multiple datasets, assessing the naturalness of the synthesized speech through human evaluation and objective metrics. Additionally, we calculate the similarity between the speech and the original audio inputs using the Speech-Similarity Learning metric.

This study aims to analyze and evaluate a proposed model of the universe's evolution based on the concept of fractional energy density, and to explore its implications for the universe's expansion history. By comparing the fractional model with standard models of a Lambda-CDM universe, this research seeks to determine its potential as a descriptor of dark energy. Key findings indicate that the maximum fractional model value of 2/3 is an upper limit for a realistic Lambda-CDM universe description, and that any measured value exceeding this threshold suggests a transitional period in the universe's expansion. Furthermore, this comparison reveals that any maximum fractional model value below 0.631 is inconsistent with current observations of a Lambda-CDM universe.

Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming problems are challenging to solve and finding suitable solutions is difficult. A new strategy, combining branch-and-bound with NSGA-II, has been developed to address these problems efficiently. This approach was tested against NSGA-II and MOBOBB using a dataset of 34 standard test cases. Results show that BnB-NSGAII produces better solution fronts, with more diversity and better extremity points, outperforming the comparison methods.

We establish a connection between two types of Lie groupoids, comparing their intrinsic properties to ensure that key features are maintained when passing from a standard definition to an internal one. Specifically, the connectedness condition is characterized by a condition that ensures path-connectedness, while a morphism is characterized by a condition that ensures agreement with its internal counterpart's level of connectedness. Notably, the connectedness conditions are not equivalent in the case of internal groupoids. We also explore internal categories and internal groupoids in the context of internal Riemann manifolds, along with a related internal version of the Cartan development map.

The Dynaswap project has developed a comprehensive cybersecurity framework for a cyberphysical system that simulates a power grid with embedded drones. This system, known as Dynaswap, incorporates a multi-layered defense mechanism comprising real-time cyber monitoring, secure data transfer, and advanced drone control. It also features a sophisticated algorithm that uses machine learning to detect and mitigate malicious activities within the system.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on uncovering both the implicit sentiment that unexpressed emotions can convey and the various forms of explicit sentiment expressed through words. The concept of implicit sentiment is illustrated by a word like "delight," which inherently suggests a sense of joy without directly stating it. In contrast, explicit sentiment encompasses a broader range of emotions, including words that convey joy, such as "thrilled," as well as words that express a more neutral form of happiness, like "happy." Our approach to detecting implicit and explicit sentiment involves a novel, data-driven technique that utilizes the concept of sentiment intensity. This method draws upon a graph-based model that categorizes words into positive, negative, and neutral groups, and assigns an intensity value to each category. By training a classifier to detect words that fall into the positive, negative, or neutral categories, and a separate classifier to assess the intensity of these emotions, we achieve a comprehensive understanding of sentiment within a text. Our experiments on public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in identifying both implicit and explicit sentiment with a notable accuracy rate of 70.80%.

We suggest a new method to calculate the most effective linear regression coefficients for continuous outcomes in a complex stratified case-control study that considers interactions between exposure and confounding variables. Although we initially present this approach for continuous variables, we also provide a solution for binary variables. Subsequently, we develop an innovative method to decompose linear regression coefficients in binary outcomes within a stratified case-control design that accounts for binary exposure and multiple binary confounding variables. We demonstrate the applicability of these methods through a real dataset analysis, a simulation study, and a guideline for effect decomposition in public health research that utilizes stratified case-control data.

This paper examines a green RIS-assisted communication network where an active RIS is employed to enhance signal strength for users. The system design problem is formulated with the goal of minimizing power consumption while ensuring users meet their requirements. This involves optimizing beamforming and phase shifts to produce a zero direct path signal from the base station, subject to power constraints. A two-step solution method is proposed, where the beamforming and phase shifts are optimized in sequence. This results in an efficient power allocation strategy that minimizes power consumption. Numerical results demonstrate the significant improvements achieved by the proposed method in terms of power efficiency.

The development of efficient lifelong learning models that can continuously learn from experience is a major goal in the field of artificial intelligence. The challenge of few-shot continual learning, where models are required to adapt to new tasks with limited data, remains a critical problem. To overcome this hurdle, we have developed a new approach that focuses on improving executive function to support ongoing learning. Our approach, known as EV-CL, combines a set of four distinct methods to enhance a model's ability to plan, control impulses, and use external memory systems to store and retrieve relevant information. Through comprehensive experiments, we have demonstrated that EV-CL outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of few-shot continual learning performance.

The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) is currently undertaking its sixth long-duration mission, providing an unprecedented opportunity to study the solar wind in close proximity to the Sun. This extended observation period will enable a comprehensive analysis of solar wind energy distributions near 0.2 astronomical units from the Sun. Previous studies have demonstrated that solar wind particle energy fluxes follow power-law distributions, with average slopes of -5.5, -4.5, and -3.5 for kinetic, thermal, and nonthermal energy, respectively. This research aims to determine the variability of these power-law characteristics during the latest long-duration observation campaign. Data from the Low Energy Magnetospheric Particle Spectrometer and Sensor (LEMPSS) and the Solar Wind Electron, Ion, and Alpha Particle (SWEAP) instrument suite were used to compute power-law slopes for kinetic, thermal, and nonthermal energy, as well as total energy, for every 90-minute interval. This study reveals significant variations in the observed power-law slopes from one interval to the next, with average kinetic, thermal, and nonthermal energy slopes of -5.2, -4.8, and -3.0, respectively, for the current observation period. This research also provides insights into the relationship between solar wind power-law slopes and radial distance from the Sun, as well as solar activity levels.

In noncommutative geometry, understanding the properties of G-C*-algebras that are locally compact and unital is crucial. This paper focuses on the classification of these algebras that are locally trivial as extensions of compact C*-algebras. The result shows that any such algebra can be represented as an induced algebra from a compact G-C*-algebra that is stabilised by the action of G. The paper also extends this result to the case of locally free actions of locally compact and amenable groups on compact manifolds. This is achieved by representing these algebras as continuous sections of a compact bundle.

We demonstrate the existence of P-maximal and P-minimal families in the context of the base hypothesis, providing distinct countablemad families with unique closure properties under forcing that preserve cardinals. Specifically, we identify two distinct countablemad families, each exhibiting contrasting resilience to forcing transformations, thereby yielding two separate consistency results that demonstrate the possibility of either minimal or maximal stable families under uncountable countable-to-countable forcing of any nontrivial countablequasiregular type.

In order to explore the potential of quantum deformation in optimizing optomechanical systems, we examine the behavior of deformed phase transitions in optical and phononic sub-systems within a three-dimensional optomechanical cavity. Our findings reveal that the introduction of deformation in the mechanical sector can lead to two distinct types of phase transitions, whereas in the optical section, it may only give rise to one. Furthermore, the investigation into parameter space indicates that near a critical point, the emergence of new energy scales associated with quantum deformation may facilitate enhanced optomechanical coupling.

In a One-Rotator Model, we've established that a classical body can be described as an R-positive scissors state. Introducing a second rotator to create a Two-Rotors Model, we've found that the scissors state becomes R-negative, exhibiting a significant decrease in the magnetic moment of the lowest scissors state. We've demonstrated that the magnitude of this magnetic moment reduction is directly proportional to the strength of coupling between the two rotators. Moreover, we've observed that the rotational barrier can be overcome by the scissors state, resulting in the appearance of a tunneling component in the wave function.

A new method using cell-averages based neural networks is proposed to solve initial boundary value problems for hyperbolic conservation laws. By training a neural network to map initial conditions to numerical solutions, the method can quickly provide solutions within a short time. It is shown that this approach is stable, and the neural network can be used to extend solutions over time by iteratively mapping the last solution to the next. When combined with a high-resolution finite volume method, this approach yields an accurate and efficient solver. The method is shown to have significant improvements in terms of allowing larger time steps compared to traditional methods, and it is able to handle discontinuities without oscillations. The method is also adaptive, the neural network can be trained once and used for various problems, and it is applicable to various systems of conservation laws.

The ALICE experiment has been working on upgrading its silicon detector to gain deeper insights into heavy-ion collisions. The primary goal of this upgrade is to utilize the new detector to make precise measurements of heavy-flavor production and the low-mass dielectron region. This article will discuss the current status of the upgrade project and provide an overview of the experiment's goals for the near future.

The Unruh effect, a phenomenon where an accelerating observer perceives a different quantum state due to their motion, has been extensively studied in the context of flat spacetime. However, the understanding of this effect in curved spacetime remains incomplete. This work delves into the Unruh effect within the framework of Einstein-Yang-Mills theory, a model of curved spacetime filled with dynamical Yang-Mills fields. We derive the Hartle-Hawking-Bunch-Davies state for the EM theory in the context of global de Sitter space, and then examine the behavior of this state under de Sitter instanton transformations. Our analysis reveals that these transformations yield distinct states, thereby providing a framework for de Sitter instanton-perturbed states. This work sets the stage for further research into the Unruh effect and the behavior of quantum fields in the context of expanding de Sitter spacetime.

One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves discovering event occurrences along with their key components within a given text. This paper introduces a novel, context-dependent approach to Event Extraction utilizing a BERT-based model. Furthermore, a substantial dataset has been developed and made available for multiple datasets, which exhibits a diverse range of events. In addition, a large-scale dataset has been constructed to test and evaluate a diverse range of languages. Our proposed method has demonstrated superior performance across English, German, and Multi language datasets in comparison to existing state-of-the-art models.
This note provides a proof of the Jacobi-Trudi identity utilizing the properties of the wedge product differential form.

The behavior of high mass X-ray binaries in extended disc systems is influenced by the presence of a stellar wind, which can be detected in the form of variable X-ray emissions. Our analysis of the 100-day light curve from the high mass X-ray binary 4U 1907+097, which is in a high and very variable hard state, reveals a strong positive correlation between wind-driven variability and X-ray fractional power in specific energy bands. Specifically, we found that this correlation is most pronounced in 10-20 Hz and 20-40 Hz frequency bands. Our results also indicate that, while X-ray fractional power is generally higher in softer states, it is comparable in the hard state of 4U 1907+097 to that of other high/low state X-ray binaries. Furthermore, we observed that X-ray fractional power in 4U 1907+097 is significantly lower than in super-Eddington X-ray binaries.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed in the non-abelian case with an aether term that transforms like a gauge field, but its space-like nature prevents it from being a proper gauge connection. The gauge symmetry and renormalizability are both preserved by the aether term's introduction. The UV behavior of the UV regulator is also examined in the context of dimensional regularization.

We examine the potential for combining syntax and semantics models, particularly in the context of the CoNLL 2022 shared task. Several JADWIG participants tested the effects of jointly modeling these tasks, with research models, like the CrossFit participant's approach, yielding optimal results on certain datasets. Nonetheless, the top professional entry from certain teams achieved better outcomes without jointly addressing these tasks, with commonalities in pre and post-processing methods contributing to the top team performance.

The relationship between the angular momentum of black holes and the mass ejected during the merger of binary black holes is examined using a set of 150 binary black hole simulations. These simulations cover a range of masses and include various configurations of the binary's orbital angular momentum and spin axes. It is discovered that the spin of the black holes plays a significant role in determining the mass ejected during the merger, with masses of the spin axes having a lesser effect. These orbital and spin characteristics are uniquely linked, which can lead to biases in the inferred relationship between mass ejected and the mass of the final black hole if not properly accounted for. However, when the correlations are properly considered, it is found that masses of ejected matter generally decrease as the mass of the final black hole increases. Moreover, it is discovered that masses of ejected matter show a significant correlation with the difference in the masses of the black holes in the binary, which can have implications for the detection of such systems using gravitational waves.

A thorough investigation of tidal features in the Dracones supergroup has been conducted, analyzing a comprehensive catalog of 1011 galaxies in the $g$-band from the SDSS DR14. This study focused on 101 massive early-type galaxies ($M_{\rm{B}} < -18.5$ mag) within the Dracones supergroup, which includes 119 tidal features. A subset of 101 massive early-type galaxies from the same volume was also examined, revealing 119 tidal features. The analysis showed that tidal features account for a significant fraction of massive early-type galaxies within $1.5$ Mpc of the Virgo cluster. Additionally, a higher incidence of tidal features among the Dracones sample compared to control samples suggests that this is a direct consequence of their membership in the supergroup. The study further revealed that tidal features exhibit a non-uniform distribution, with tidal feature-free regions interspersed with clusters of features. This distribution aligns with the distribution of dark matter halos, suggesting that tidal features primarily result from minor mergers rather than mergers of comparable mass.

The Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation proposes a novel gravitational model, which attributes the polar regions of massive bodies to a repulsive gravitational effect, thereby representing the gravitational analog of magnetic dipoles. This effect is the result of the interaction between two distinct gravitational fields, an attractive field dominating the equatorial plane and a repulsive field dominating the polar regions. This dual-field concept is further supported by the phenomenon of orbital inclination, where a planet's orbit is inclined at an angle relative to its host star, an effect that can be explained by the interaction between these fields. This theory also has significant implications for the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation, which is a two-dimensional extension of Einstein's General Theory of Relativity.

A recent study of repeating fast radio bursts (FRBs) has led to a significant shift in our understanding of their underlying astrophysical processes.  This new perspective suggests that flare-like activity may be responsible for bursts of activity in neutron star systems.  To explore this possibility, we have proposed a multi-stage model of an explosive event in a young neutron star system, which could produce bursts of activity similar to those seen in astrophysical phenomena.  This new model suggests that neutron star systems may undergo a series of explosive events, which could be triggered by changes in the local magnetic field.  This new model could potentially explain the observed properties of FRBs, including their periodic bursts of activity and the associated gamma-ray bursts.

A comprehensive review is presented, detailing the latest advancements in a
highly versatile research platform, integrated laser system, capable of
accomplishing a broad spectrum of tasks. The research platform, with its
broad application scope, has found significant roles in industrial,
technological, defense, space, and other domains. The platform's potential
applications, including but not limited to CPA, NLO, frequency comb,
all-optical switching, and more, are thoroughly explored and explained.

Recent advancements in image-guided text generation have achieved impressive results, yet existing methods face challenges in handling arbitrary input images and producing lengthy, high-quality captions. To overcome these limitations, we present MAGIC, a novel framework that leverages dense visual tokens to capture both local and global image features. By utilizing sparse semantic prompts, MAGIC effectively filters out extraneous token information and focuses on critical semantic aspects. By integrating the dense MAGIC image representation with the sparse semantic token, the model generates detailed captions enriched with visual and semantic information. Experiments on a variety of datasets demonstrate MAGIC's superior performance in aligning with input images and producing high-quality captions, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, MAGIC's innovative approach enables it to generate high-quality captions for complex inputs, including multi-panel images and diagrams. The code for MAGIC is available at the link below.

We present an innovative, practical breakthrough in Delegated RingCT, a groundbreaking cryptographic method for anonymous transaction verification in decentralized cryptocurrencies. Our proposed solution efficiently verifies transactions within a reasonable timeframe, even when the sender of an anonymous transaction is not directly involved in the process. This advancement builds upon existing ringCT protocols, which have been hindered by their inherent limitations in scalability and computational efficiency.

In the field of particle physics, researchers utilize a technique called emittance scans to measure the spatial spread of a particle beam at a collider. These scans are essential in understanding beam dynamics, but existing methods to measure emittance are often time-consuming and can't't be performed frequently enough. A new, automated system has been developed to perform repeated scans quickly, in as little as 10 minutes. This new design is being implemented in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and is set to play a crucial role in upgrading the collider to increase its luminosity in the High-Luminosity LHC phase.

One of the most pressing challenges in artificial neural networks is catastrophic forgetting, a significant obstacle to continual learning. This phenomenon occurs when a model trained on a new task loses its previous knowledge. Researchers have been exploring various methods to overcome this issue, with the most recent approach focusing on regularizing artificial neural networks to retain previous tasks. This paper examines the effectiveness of such regularization methods in relation to the well-established Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) algorithm. Our investigation reveals that regularization techniques can be detrimental to model performance and that their benefits are limited to very shallow networks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ECW's proposed solution to a related problem of non-differentiable regularization is not universally applicable.

Using data collected at a center-of-mass energy of 10.52 GeV, a dataset of 2.49 fb^-1 was obtained from the BESIII experiment. The production cross-sections for the decays J/psi to gamma gamma' and psi(2s) to gamma gamma' were measured in conjunction with gamma gamma' decay into K+ K- and were found to be 1.1 pb and 0.4 pb, respectively. The branching ratios for gamma gamma' decay into K+ K- were determined to be 10.1% and 0.14% for gamma gamma' and psi(2s), respectively. The observed discrepancies between these results and previous studies were statistically significant.

Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in numerous applications, yet its high computational requirements and memory usage pose a significant challenge for widespread adoption. To address this, researchers have been exploring various techniques to reduce the size and computational demands of deep neural networks, thereby facilitating their deployment on a broader range of devices. One of these approaches, quantized neural networks, involves reducing the precision of learned parameters, which can significantly decrease the storage needs and computational costs. In this work, we provide a comprehensive overview of the principles and implementations of quantized neural networks, including an examination of the effects of quantization on the training process and the development of effective strategies for mitigating these issues. Additionally, we discuss the effective use of quantized weights and activations in improving model performance. Finally, we highlight the potential of quantized neural networks in achieving energy-efficient and scalable deep learning applications.

The intrinsic robot's flexibility and the soft robot's inherent nonlinearity and anisotropy make modeling its behavior a complex and challenging task. Despite the existing models, they often require significant computational resources and a deep understanding of material properties. In an effort to overcome these hurdles, a new, data-driven model has been developed using machine learning techniques. The new model combines the use of neural networks with the finite element method to create a more efficient and accurate simulation. The results of the study show that the new model is able to accurately predict the behavior of the robot under different conditions, and that the level of prediction can be further improved by incorporating more real-world data.

The Jacobi group $G^J_1(\mathbb{R})$ is formed as a semidirect product of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ and the Heisenberg group, with the Heisenberg group acting on $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ via automorphisms. This group can be viewed as an extension of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ by the Heisenberg group, with its Lie algebra being a semidirect sum. This mathematical structure is explored in depth, with an investigation into its representation theory and connection to Heisenberg group representations. This process leads to a parameterized family of irreducible representations of the Jacobi algebra that are not unitary in nature. This newly discovered set of representations significantly enhances the well-known Schrödinger representation theory.

Verifying facts using structured data is crucial in various fields, such as fact-checking and automated question-answering. The main obstacle in this area is integrating and interpreting diverse structured data, such as tables and knowledge graphs. The Table RAG model overcomes this challenge by using a fine-tuned BERT query encoder to extract relevant information from a structured knowledge graph and a tabular data repository. The model then generates a set of subgraphs and multiple table queries to gather supporting or refuting evidence. The information is passed through a summarization layer, which combines multiple queries and related evidence to answer a given question. The model's output is a verification score indicating the accuracy of the provided statement, which is evaluated against a structured data reference. The model's results demonstrate its effectiveness in fact verification tasks.

The choice between supervised and unsupervised methods for synthetic image generation is a common issue in computer vision.  Although unsupervised methods have the advantage of not requiring labeled data, they are often plagued by issues such as mode collapse and inferior generative capabilities.  On the other hand, supervised methods are more effective but require a labor-intensive process of creating a large, high-quality dataset.  To address this challenge, we propose a new approach that leverages unsupervised image generation techniques in conjunction with weak annotations to create synthetic images.  By starting with a pre-trained generator, we can avoid the need for a large dataset and instead rely on weak annotations to create synthetic images.  Our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both generative capabilities and diversity.

We introduce a versatile and efficient method for tackling complex, high-dimensional statistical inference issues. Building on the success of differential evolution algorithms in global optimization, our proposed approach utilizes transformations to adapt this technique for sampling from intricate, high-dimensional distributions. This method exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms, particularly in cases involving a large number of parameters. A key benefit of using differential-based sampling is its simplicity, as it only requires a numerical multivariate integrator. This feature makes our approach highly attractive for problems where traditional sampling techniques may struggle, such as those involving latent variables. We extensively evaluate the efficacy of our proposed approach through a series of numerical experiments, including its application to the estimation of the bivariate normal copula density, the inference of parameters in a complex hierarchical model, and the inference of parameters in a complex mixture model.

In fault-tolerant distance labeling, we seek a set of distance labels for every node in a graph, allowing us to determine the shortest path between any two connected nodes, even when one node is faulty. We focus on short labeling schemes that work efficiently, with a linear time complexity for computation and labels whose size depends logarithmically on the total number of nodes. We develop a general framework for creating these labeling schemes, specifically for graphs with chordal proofs and metrical box structures, and apply it to create labels for all edges in a graph, with labels no larger than 10 times the square of log n. Additionally, we show that any fault-tolerant labeling scheme for all edges in a graph, with labels not exceeding a certain complexity, implies a labeling scheme for all pairs of nodes, with pairs restricted to a triple of nodes, and that this lower bound is a fundamental constraint.

We have developed a novel method to calculate two-particle correlation functions in the context of the three-color model with periodic boundary conditions. Utilizing a combination of numerical and analytical techniques, we have successfully computed the model's two-particle correlations for any model parameter value. To achieve this, we have utilized an expansion of the model's non-zero eigenvalue and eigenimaginary part of the Liouvillian, which oscillate at frequencies determined by the model's eigenvalues. Notably, the model exhibits a first-order phase transition characterized by a discontinuous change in the model's eigenvalues, which governs the model's behavior in its different phases. In the model's various phases, the model's eigenvalues dictate the model's asymptotic behavior of correlation functions, including a power-law decay rate and a characteristic frequency of oscillations.

For a given second-order linear elliptic equation with coefficients $A_{ij}$ and a function $f$, we establish that a weak solution $u$ exists and is unique under the conditions that $A_{ij}$ is bounded by $C$ and $\omega$-H\"older continuous by $[\omega]$, while $f$ is $\beta$-H\"older continuous, where the exponents $\beta$, $\omega$, and the constant $C$ collectively satisfy the inequality $2\beta + \omega > 1$. We demonstrate that the solution $u$ possesses second-order derivatives that are $\beta$H\"older continuous throughout the domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, with the method involving the construction of a smooth approximation of $u$ and an a priori estimate that incorporates the $\omega$-H\"older continuity of the coefficients $A_{ij}$.

In medical imaging tasks, out-of-distribution detection is crucial for ensuring the reliability of AI models. We present a novel framework, named LiGHT, that enhances out-of-distribution detection in medical image analysis. LiGHT leverages local and global features to distinguish between variations in data and inherent out-of-distribution content. By utilizing a multi-scale feature disentanglement approach, LiGHT isolates semantic variations and identifies local anomalies. The experimental results demonstrate that LiGHT excels in accurately identifying normal data and providing robust out-of-distribution detection.

In a driven open quantum system coupled to a thermal bath, the system's state is described by a steady state that remains unchanged over time. It has been observed that certain phases of the system are characterized by abrupt changes in the steady state when the driving force is gradually altered. This phenomenon is referred to as a "quantum quench." This article focuses on an experimentally feasible model for studying quantum quenches in an open system, which mimics a quantum spin model consisting of two spin-1/2 particles and a bath of N two-level atoms. The thermal bath is created through incoherent excitation of a continuous wave source, which is then dissipated via spontaneous emission. This approach allows researchers to explore a type of quantum quench that occurs when the thermal state of the bath is decoupled from the system, which is characterized by an order parameter that marks the transition between ordered and disordered phases.

The article explores the convex solution $u$ of a non-linear elliptic equation with a non-divergence form in an open, bounded area of complex plane, where a specific weighted Dirichlet problem is considered with the boundary conditions being zero. An investigation of key properties of $u$ and its convex gradient $
abla u$ follows, where it's demonstrated that the Alexandrov maximum principle and H"older continuity of $u$ and $
abla u$ are contingent upon the H"older continuity of the Hessian of $u$. Furthermore, it's shown that the gradient $
abla u$ converges uniformly in all compact sub-domains of the boundary data as it approaches the zero boundary data, where the zero boundary data is in the H"older class. The analysis also includes the convex solution of the non-divergence weighted Dirichlet problem with a non-linear elliptic equation, where the zero boundary data is in the H"older class.

Counting the recurrence of periodic events allows us to measure time. However, in some stochastic processes like clicking neurons, it may be possible to design clocks that become periodic on a larger timescale. We propose a new clock concept that can be applied to both periodic events and stochastic processes. This versatile timer can be implemented using various physical systems that exhibit regular or random behavior. We develop a universal model for these devices and compare its accuracy to traditional periodic timers. This model is demonstrated with a neuron that has a simple two-state model. We find that the random nature of these timers can lead to inaccuracies, which can be calculated using the central limit theorem. We also show that the random error can be determined without knowing the full probability distribution, which is an advantage. This method is further illustrated with a neuron that has a more realistic model.

This research explores the integration of Fog computing with Software Defined Networks (SDN) to overcome the Fog-SDN challenges identified in the existing literature. The proposed solution involves four key aspects: (1) minimizing latency, (2) reducing network congestion, (3) maintaining data security, and (4 enhancing energy efficiency. To address these challenges, a novel Fog-SDN architecture has been designed, featuring a centralized controller, multiple Gateways, and distributed Fogs. This work also delves into the essential components of Fog-SDN, including network management, service management, Fog-SDN controllers, and the Open Fog Reference Architecture (OFG-Ref-Arch). Furthermore, the paper discusses the selection of Fog-SDN gateways and evaluates Fog-SDN as a viable approach for Fog computing.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is designed to establish a mapping between data points that preserves the underlying distances. In the context of image retrieval, a pair-wise loss function is optimized to produce an image embedding that enhances retrieval accuracy. Typically, a greedy approach is employed, where the local gradients of the pair-wise loss with respect to the model's parameters are assumed to accurately reflect the true direction towards the optimal solution. However, this assumption may not always hold, as the focus on individual metrics may hinder overall optimization. Consequently, the optimization process can become inefficient, especially when conflicts arise between the learned metrics. To address this limitation, a novel method, Meta learning, is proposed to synthesize pair-wise gradients into a unified direction towards the optimal solution, thereby accelerating the optimization process and improving retrieval performance. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of Meta learning in a variety of tasks, where it outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods.

Recent studies have shown that certain holographic tensor networks can effectively implement quantum error correction due to their inherent geometric characteristics, which facilitate successful teleportation and entanglement recovery following errors. This research demonstrates that these properties can be directly harnessed for quantum computation by creating output states that correct for errors. The proposed network, specifically the $\alpha$-MERA, is capable of computing two-qubit gates on an arbitrary number of qubits with a code distance that increases linearly with the number of qubits. Moreover, the proposed network exhibits resilience against errors in both complex phase and unitary matrix measurements. The work also outlines a protocol for recovering from errors that can be applied to any input state.

The study of Galactic center's magnetized radio filaments reveals their intriguing properties and groupings. The research focuses on these unique structures, which exhibit distinct features, such as beading and branching, and are found to be 10-100 times brighter than other similar radio filaments. The analysis of their polarized emission and magnetic field orientation, along with the correlation between surface brightness and polarization, provides insights into their formation and potential mechanisms. The study also discusses the possible connection between these groupings and other phenomena, such as jets and outflows, and their relation to other galaxies' radio filaments.

A proposed paper introduces a new method for enhancing conservation voltage reduction (CVR) algorithm accuracy through the integration of machine learning. The current approach involves a two-step process: initially, the power flow equations are solved to determine node voltages and line flows, and then, the average voltage is used to calculate load reduction. In contrast, the new method leverages the relationship between voltage and load reduction by utilizing an artificial neural network (ANN) trained on power flow data. The method's accuracy is validated through simulations on the IEEE 13-bus and IEEE 33-bus systems, and the results demonstrate its reliability and ease of implementation.

We examine non-stochastic bandits and experts in a delayed context, where delayed rewards and losses are considered. The delayed settings are complicated by the fact that actions must be taken based on past information, making them challenging for algorithm designers. We develop a novel algorithm that effectively addresses delayed feedback in both pure and delayed feedback scenarios, while also exposing a trade-off between competitive ratios and algorithmic delays. This discovery contrasts with the non-delayed case, where competitive ratios are independent of algorithmic delays. Our findings indicate that the delayed feedback case is fundamentally different from the non-delayed case, as demonstrated by a specific problem instance where non-delayed algorithms fail to achieve sublinear regret. We conclude that the delayed feedback case is a distinct and significant area of research.

In task-oriented conversations, speakers often reuse words to achieve specific goals, 
resulting in a bias towards minimal language use that reinforcement learning can amplify.
This issue is often overlooked by current dialogue systems. To counter this, we've developed a technique to boost lexical variety by incorporating the diversity of dialogue responses as a secondary goal that is consistently measured across various states, 
prioritizing responses that are both diverse and accurate. Our approach has been tested 
on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and has shown a notable 20% increase in word variety while 
maintaining the same level of precision as a standard reinforcement learning policy.

In the 1970s, quantum chromodynamics (QCD) was investigated using lattice QCD, where Kenneth Wilson developed a framework to understand the theory's non-perturbative aspects numerically. Lattice QCD combines the standard QCD action with the Euclidean metric and discretizes spacetime into a grid. Wilson's approach was initially met with skepticism, but later demonstrated the renormalization group's ability to remove cutoff dependence, proving the validity of the method. Initially, simulations at fixed temperature and finite volume were conducted to determine the phase transition, but current capabilities allow for larger simulations that can calculate physical quark masses, binding energies, and other phenomena, including the mass of the proton, quantum chromodynamics infrared slavery, and thermal phase transitions.

A key factor in predicting the loading responses to offshore wind turbines is the varying uncertainty in environmental conditions, which can be represented by the conditional heteroscedasticity in meteo-ocean data. To account for this, a novel approach has been developed to simulate the time series of wind speed and wave height, taking into consideration the uncertainty associated with them. This approach involves training a deep generative model on meteo-ocean data and online updating the time series based on the turbine's structural condition. To achieve this, a variational autoencoder is used to encode the meteo-ocean data and a Q-learning agent is employed to update the encoder online. This approach has been shown to effectively reduce uncertainty in the load predictions and outperform traditional methods in terms of accuracy and reliability.

The devastating 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami in Japan, along with a massive nuclear disaster, highlighted the significant impact social media can have on disaster management and public relations. To effectively communicate with a large audience, organizations like the Japanese government rely on Twitter, but they often struggle to gauge public sentiment accurately. In this context, we present a groundbreaking approach to monitor public opinion during natural disasters by combining a time-sensitive sentiment analysis model with a long-term baseline. The proposed method aims to track the real-time fluctuations of public sentiment by analyzing recent Twitter posts, while also accounting for the underlying sentiment over a longer period. By comparing the sentiment of recent posts to a baseline established from historical data, this approach enables a more comprehensive understanding of public opinion during and after a disaster.

A group G possesses the R_n property if for every element gamma in G with n centralized twisted conjugacy classes, the corresponding centralizer of gamma is not trivial. We examine the influence of the ring's characteristic on Gaussian G-Lasky groups in gaining the R_n property by comparing them with their generalized general linear group counterparts. Additionally, we identify conditions under which group extensions can acquire the R_n property. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the R_n property and generalized K-theory by connecting it to the twisted K_0-group of the group with trivial action.

A novel, step-by-step approach to analyzing time-resolved data is developed.
This technique relies on two key principles: the first involves a constraint
ensuring the continuity of a model's representation of time-dependent data,
while the second employs a regularization method tailored to the structure of
data that changes over time.
To demonstrate the method's effectiveness, we apply it to a dataset from a
pulsed neutron scattering study of an under-cooled liquid.
Our results show that the method produces highly detailed, physically grounded
findings, significantly outperforming existing, widely used techniques.

This paper introduces the SceNDD, a groundbreaking naturalistic driving dataset designed specifically for advanced scene understanding and complex signal processing. The SceNDD was collected using a specialized vehicle equipped with various sensors, including multiple cameras capturing diverse perspectives of the driving environment, and an integrated GPS system to track the driver's actions and navigation decisions. The comprehensive dataset includes high-resolution images, audio recordings, and precise geographical data, collected during 40 hours of driving across 12 locations. The rich dataset is available for download at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch-DarwinX/datasets SceNDD.

In connection with the Almiray-Bennett-Preskill-Winter theory of entanglement recovery, our analysis reveals an entanglement recovery scenario, which is analogous to the restoration of entanglement in subsystems, for a partition of subsystems within a larger set. This phenomenon is inextricably linked to a specific configuration known as the entanglement wedge cross section. We demonstrate that this cross section area is proportional to the reflected entropy of corresponding subsystems, a relationship analogous to results from conformal field theory. This relationship also connects to a specific cross section area that arises from applying the double trace flow to holographic duals of conformal field theories.

Recent studies have shown that reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) can greatly enhance the capabilities of orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems by allowing for the management of the propagation environment and the creation of optimal channels. However, the RIS-aided OFDM system's performance relies heavily on the phase shifters' accuracy in the reflective phase shifter (RPS) architecture, particularly when the channel estimation process is affected by imperfect channel state information. To address this issue, a novel RIS-aided OFDM system is proposed, incorporating a two-step channel estimation algorithm based on iterative minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimation. This innovative approach effectively mitigates the adverse effects of imperfect channel state information, thereby enhancing the system's ability to adapt to dynamic environments. Furthermore, a closed-form expression for the achievable sum-rate is derived, providing valuable insights into the trade-offs between the number of phase shifters and the system's overall performance.

We examine the impact of energy meter limitations on the accuracy of the Hamiltonian, a quantum system's governing energy function. Building on prior research that focused on idealized meters, we incorporate the real-world constraints of quantum devices, specifically their finite resolution. This refinement reveals how the meter's ability to distinguish between different energy levels affects its performance, which is quantified by the average squared error in the energy function's estimation. Notably, this error can decrease without bound as the meter's resolution improves, but only up to a certain point determined by the distinctiveness between the system's energy levels. We also demonstrate the applicability of our findings in the specific case of qubits, the fundamental units of quantum computing.

We have established a connection between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, as well as an exploration of soliton properties with G2 symmetry. Additionally, we have derived a formula for calculating Laplacian cocycles associated with differential forms, leveraging cohomology arguments and the Fritzsch formula. This approach is exemplified by calculations for 1-forms and Kähler 2-forms in both G2 and U(n) geometries.

Public health officials are employing contact tracing to curb the spread of contagious diseases. This method aims to pinpoint individuals who may have been exposed to an infected person and prevent further transmission. To combat the COVID-19 pandemic, tech companies have developed contact tracing apps that raise significant privacy issues due to the massive collection of sensitive personal data. This report delves into the data collection practices of popular contact tracing apps, sheds light on the data's sensitivity, and discusses the potential consequences of data breaches. Furthermore, it explores the implications of app data usage and offers recommendations on how to mitigate privacy risks.

The main objective of this work is to examine the connection between quantum correlations and classical statistical correlations. We aim to clarify how the concept of quantum entanglement relates to significant correlations observed in classical statistics. We demonstrate that the correlations in classical statistics arise from a combination of quantum entanglement and an additional factor that accounts for intrinsic properties of the ensemble under consideration.

A programming language's syntax is formalized using the Backus-Naur Form (BNF), which is then used to generate corresponding syntax trees via a code generator, and the bison tool. BNF is subsequently extended with additional constructs to accommodate Babel, resulting in a modified BNF that is used to generate enhanced syntax trees via bison, and bison tools. Additionally, bison tools are supplemented to incorporate new functionalities that facilitate Babel's functionality. Furthermore, bison tools are further enhanced to incorporate new functionalities that facilitate Babel's functionality.
